wildfireMethodology:
SCOPE & THRESHOLD (updated per user request)
This version includes every wildfire >10,000 acres in size that this research pass could identify
within roughly 50 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail corridor, from 2000 through mid-2026. It replaces
the earlier "curated significant fires" version, which was judged too selective (it omitted the
2024 Park Fire, among others -- now corrected and included).

HOW THIS LIST WAS BUILT
1. California: worked year-by-year (2000-2026) through CAL FIRE's official "large fires" lists,
   as compiled in each year's Wikipedia wildfire-season article (e.g. "2013 California wildfires"),
   cross-checked directly against CAL FIRE's own incident archive (fire.ca.gov/incidents/<year>)
   where that data was cleanly available (2015, 2016, 2017, 2021, 2022).
2. Oregon & Washington: no single equivalent year-by-year public list exists, so this pass combined
   (a) Wikipedia's state wildfire-season articles for available years, and (b) the US Forest Service
   Pacific Northwest Region's official annual wildfire summaries, which rank each year's largest
   fires by National Forest -- a very reliable primary source, but one that is normally only
   published for the biggest years (2017, 2018, 2020, 2021, 2024, 2025 were checked this session;
   2016, 2019 were not independently checked and may contain additional qualifying fires).
3. Every fire >=10,000 acres found in a PCT-adjacent county or National Forest was included, with
   name, year, acreage, cause, structures, and damage pulled from that fire's own Wikipedia page or
   CAL FIRE/InciWeb incident page where available.

WHAT "PCT-ADJACENT" MEANT IN PRACTICE
Rather than measuring exact distance for all 200+ fires (which would require GIS work beyond this
research pass), fires were included/excluded by county and National Forest against the trail's
known route: Cleveland, San Bernardino, Angeles, Sequoia, Sierra, Inyo, Stanislaus, Eldorado, Tahoe,
Plumas, Lassen, Shasta-Trinity and Klamath National Forests in California; Rogue River-Siskiyou,
Fremont-Winema, Umpqua, Willamette, Deschutes, and Mt. Hood National Forests in Oregon; and Gifford
Pinchot, Okanogan-Wenatchee, and Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forests plus North Cascades National
Park in Washington. Fires in counties/forests that only partly overlap this corridor, or that
straddle a genuinely large county (e.g. Trinity, San Bernardino, Siskiyou), are flagged in the
"Data Confidence" column as NEEDS DISTANCE VERIFICATION -- this is not a guess that they're outside
50 miles, just an honest flag that this pass didn't confirm the precise distance. Rows shaded amber
carry this flag. Please treat the county/coordinate-based screening as a strong first pass, not a
survey-grade answer -- true perimeter-to-trail distance should ultimately come from GIS (see below).

DATA QUALITY NOTES (carried over and expanded from v1)
- Latitude/longitude for the 185 newly added fires are COUNTY/NATIONAL FOREST CENTROIDS, not fire
  ignition points -- deliberately conservative approximations, clearly less precise than the 22
  fires researched individually in the first pass (which use each fire's actual reported coordinates).
  Do not plot these as precise map pins; use them only to sort/filter by rough geography.
- "Approx. PCT Mile" is illustrative only (measured northbound from the US/Mexico border at Campo, CA).
- Cause, structures, and fatalities for the newly added fires are only populated when that detail
  was explicitly present in the source table's notes column; blanks mean "not stated in that
  source," not "zero" or "unknown to have occurred."
- Financial damage is populated only where a source explicitly gave a dollar figure; as in v1, this
  mixes total economic loss, suppression cost, settlements, and restitution -- do not sum this column.
- A handful of very large, well-known fires (Camp Fire, Palisades Fire, Eaton Fire, Hughes Fire,
  Chetco Bar Fire, Flat Fire 2023) are included with an explicit flag because their core burn area is
  arguably outside the 50-mile corridor (coastal Los Angeles basin, or coastal SW Oregon) even though
  the county touches PCT-adjacent National Forest land elsewhere. Use judgment on whether to keep
  them in your storyline.
- Some 2018-2019 and 2023 Oregon/Washington seasons were comparatively quiet and were checked but
  yielded no additional qualifying fires beyond what's listed; this was confirmed by season-total
  acreage figures (e.g. 2023 Oregon: ~260,000 acres statewide, well below the threshold for a new
  megafire) rather than by exhaustively checking every named fire.

KNOWN REMAINING GAPS (be aware before treating this as exhaustive)
- 2000-2012 Oregon and Washington were not systematically checked this session (no clean equivalent
  of the CAL FIRE year-page existed to search quickly); if your storyline needs that period for OR/WA,
  it should be treated as unverified rather than "no fires occurred."
- A few multi-fire complexes mentioned in passing (e.g. Diamond Complex and Homestead Complex, Umpqua
  NF, 2024) were identified but not sized/sourced in time for this pass.
- "All fires" in the literal sense -- including the thousands under 10,000 acres -- are still not
  here by design (see v1's rationale); postholer.com/trail-fires remains the resource for that view.

RECOMMENDED NEXT STEP FOR MAP-GRADE PRECISION
For the interactive map, pull actual fire perimeter polygons (not the point coordinates in this
sheet) from NIFC/WFIGS (data-nifc.opendata.arcgis.com) and intersect them in a GIS tool against the
official PCT centerline (available from the Pacific Crest Trail Association or USFS) to get a
precise mile-by-mile "distance from trail" for every fire -- that would resolve every row currently
flagged NEEDS DISTANCE VERIFICATION in one pass.
trailPointsMethodology:
SCOPE
86 points along the Pacific Crest Trail (US/Mexico border to US/Canada border), tagged by category:
- Entry/Exit: a road, trailhead, or pass where a hiker can get on or off the trail
- Resupply: a place to buy food, mail a package, or otherwise resupply
- Landmark: a national park, wilderness area, or major geographic feature
Most rows carry more than one tag (e.g., Tuolumne Meadows is Entry/Exit + Resupply + Landmark all at once) --
use the X columns to filter for whichever list you need.

MILE MARKER SYSTEM -- IMPORTANT CAVEAT
Two different "official" mileage systems exist and don't quite agree:
1. Halfmile's Pacific Crest Trail Data (the 2023 dataset used for every mile marker in this sheet) puts the
   trail at 2,664.1 miles. This is the same underlying dataset PCTA's own website resupply map is built on
   ("mile points along the trail from the 2020 Halfmile Project dataset").
2. PCTA's own official GIS centerline, updated every January to reflect the latest reroutes, currently
   measures 2,655.78 miles (as of the 2025 update) -- roughly 8 miles shorter, due to trail relocations that
   have shortened or straightened sections since Halfmile's data was last generated. PCTA explicitly notes
   that "Halfmile's mile markers may differ from the data in this centerline due to reroutes."
This sheet uses Halfmile's northbound (NB) mileage throughout for internal consistency, since that's the
system almost all thru-hiker resources (guidebooks, apps, trail journals) still reference. Treat every mile
figure as accurate to within a mile or two, not survey-grade -- and expect real-world GPS mileage to run
a few miles short of the numbers here, especially north of the Sierra.

SOURCING BY CATEGORY
- Resupply towns: sourced directly from Halfmile's "Pacific Crest Trail Resupply & Town Notes" (pctmap.net),
  which is the exact document PCTA's own resupply page (pcta.org/.../pct-resupply-towns-locations/) points
  hikers to for detail beyond its interactive map. This covers every resupply point Mexico-to-Canada with
  services, hours, and shipping addresses as of the 2023 edition.
- Entry/Exit points: major highway crossings and trailheads, cross-referenced against Halfmile's data,
  USFS ranger-district trail pages, and PCTA/Washington Trails Association section descriptions. A few
  (Barker Pass, Ebbetts Pass, Carson Pass, Chinook Pass, Hart's Pass, Rainy Pass) are not resupply points
  but are well-documented, commonly used access points in PCT section-hiking literature.
- Landmarks: national parks, monuments, and major wilderness areas the trail passes through or near,
  identified from NPS and USFS sources for the relevant units.

KNOWN LIMITATIONS
- Mile markers for landmarks and passes that aren't resupply towns (e.g., wilderness-area boundaries,
  Forester Pass, Donohue Pass) are reasonable approximations from standard PCT trail literature, not
  independently checked against the current GIS centerline point-by-point this session.
- "Echo Lake and Palisades" (the example given in the request) is represented here as Echo Lake (mile
  1093.5) and Barker Pass (mile ~1159), which together bound the popular Lake Tahoe-area section --
  Barker Pass is the standard access point for the Tahoe City / Palisades Tahoe (formerly Squaw Valley)
  area. If a different pair of points was intended, let me know and I can adjust.
- The Canada border crossing note (northern terminus) reflects a real, current access restriction: PCTA's
  2025 data update removed the Manning Park, BC connector trail because entry into Canada at that point
  is no longer permitted. This is worth knowing for any storyline involving the northern terminus.
- This list is not literally exhaustive (PCTA's own resupply map caveat: "may not include all possible
  resupply locations") -- it's every point Halfmile's guide documents, plus the standard set of additional
  entry/exit points and landmarks used across PCT trip-planning resources.

PRIMARY SOURCES
1. Halfmile's Pacific Crest Trail Resupply & Town Notes (2023 edition) -- pctmap.net
   https://pctmap.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/halfmiles_pct_notes_resupply-1.pdf
2. PCTA -- PCT Resupply Towns & Locations -- pcta.org/discover-the-trail/thru-hiking-long-distance-hiking/resupply/pct-resupply-towns-locations/
3. PCTA -- 2025 PCT Centerline and Mile Marker Update (trail length, reroute notes, Canada border note)
4. PCTA -- PCT Data page (centerline/mile-marker GIS data, Creative Commons licensed)
5. USFS Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail homepage and ranger-district pages (Humboldt-Toiyabe,
   Okanogan-Wenatchee, Gifford Pinchot, Klamath, Deschutes, Willamette national forests)
6. Washington Trails Association -- PCT section descriptions (Chinook Pass, Snoqualmie Pass)
7. NPS unit pages -- Yosemite, Crater Lake, Mount Rainier, North Cascades
8. explore.pcta.org (PCTA's trip-planning map/trailhead tool)
